title: From a Pune Wada to 42 Countries: How Mother's Recipe Became India's Pickle Empire
excerpt: A Gujarat family that started in tobacco in a 1901 Pune wada built a pickle brand sold in 42 countries — and just repackaged all 64 varieties as 'the taste of a mother's love.'
body:
• Mother's Recipe traces its roots to a wada — a traditional Maharashtrian house — in Pune's Kasba Peth, where the Desai family's business began in 1901 before it entered food.
  • Since acquiring the brand in 2002, Desai Brothers has grown it from pickles into chutneys, pastes, spices, papads, instant mixes and ready-to-cook foods, with products now sold in more than 42 countries.
  • Acquisitions drove the expansion: Kolkata-based Elmac Agro (Rs 30 crore, 2015) brought sauces into the range, and Spreadon took the brand into spreads and dips.
  • In the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf, the full range is stocked at Indian grocery stores and on Amazon — and all 64 pickle varieties have just been repackaged with labels in regional languages under the "Swaad Mamta Ka" (taste of a mother's love) refresh.

Mother's Recipe may be best known for its pickles today, but it all began in a wada, a traditional Maharashtrian house, in Pune's Kasba Peth area. The family came to Pune from Gujarat and started its business in 1901, founded by Haribhai V. Desai — in tobacco, not food. It would take a century for the Desais to turn a family kitchen craft into one of India's most recognised packaged-food brands.

The pivot came through diversification. "At that point in time, pickles were available only in Maharashtra and a few other states. The family wanted to diversify and the food business was a growth sector we were looking at," Sanjana Desai, Head of Business Development for the Food Division, told Your Story.

Studying how India actually cooks

The family's approach was methodical rather than industrial. "My father took over the business first and I remember seeing him going to the mandis at four in the morning and checking the mangoes that went into making the pickles," Desai recalled. The team studied how people cook in different parts of India — the spices, the oils, the methods — before scaling recipes that had to taste homemade in millions of kitchens.

Desai Brothers acquired Mother's Recipe in 2002, and the portfolio has kept widening since: papad, chutneys, cooking pastes, curry powders, instant mixes, sharbat, ready-to-cook foods and sauces. In 2015 the company bought Kolkata-based Elmac Agro Manufacturing for Rs 30 crore, bringing sauces into its range, and later acquired Spreadon to enter the spreads and dips market.

The numbers tell the story of the build-out. By FY 2015-16 the brand had clocked around Rs 250 crore in revenue, with a stated target of Rs 500 crore within three years, according to Your Story's reporting. Exports have been a major engine: the brand's offerings are exported to more than 42 countries, with industry reports putting exports at roughly 40% of overall revenue at times — across the Middle East, the US, Canada, the UK, Europe, Australia and Africa.

"For generations, Mother's Recipe pickles have stood for authenticity, nostalgia, and the unmistakable flavours of mother's love."

— Sanjana Desai, Head of Business Development, Desai Brothers

Sixty-four pickles, one mother's love

Alongside its growth, the brand has leaned into the emotional shorthand of its name. All 64 pickle varieties have been repackaged under the idea of "Swaad Mamta Ka" — the taste of a mother's love. The new designs take inspiration from Indian homes: the bangles mothers wear, the colours of traditional sarees, the brass utensils found in Indian kitchens. The packs also carry the names of all 64 pickle varieties in regional languages on the labels — a small but telling recognition that a Punjabi pickle shelf looks nothing like a Tamil one.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, Mother's Recipe occupies a specific emotional slot: the jar that travels in suitcases and shows up in apartments from Edison to East Ham. The 42-country footprint means the brand is reliably stocked in Indian grocery stores across the US, Canada, the UK and the Gulf, as well as on Amazon and its own e-store. If you're hunting the new packaging, look for the regional-language variety names — the relaunch makes it easier to find the exact achar you grew up with.

What's next

The trajectory points to a brand chasing the ready-to-cook and instant-mix categories as hard as it once chased pickles, with HORECA and food-service verticals as the next growth bet. The bet is that "mother's taste" scales — and a century after the Kasba Peth wada, the Desais are still selling the idea that it does.
